title: Pain That Makes Her Vomit

patient.name: Mdm Devi d/o Ramasamy
patient.presenting_complaint: Severe right eye pain with headache and nausea that started this evening

history.hpc: Mdm Devi presents with severe right eye pain that began a few hours ago. She says: 'My eye very pain, like someone press very hard, until I want to vomit, and my head also pain.' She rates the pain 9/10. She reports seeing haloes around lights and her vision is blurred. She feels nauseated and has vomited once. Bright light worsens the discomfort.
history.pmhx: Hyperopia (long-sighted). Otherwise well. No previous eye conditions.
history.social_hx: Lives with family. Brought in by her daughter this evening.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right eye: red, hazy/cloudy cornea, mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil. Left eye: normal.
examination_findings.fundus: Right fundus view poor due to corneal haze

investigations.pain_assessment_history: Structured pain history: severity 9/10, deep pressing pain in and around the right eye, associated headache, nausea and vomiting, haloes around lights, photophobia, and blurred vision. This symptom cluster (severe pain + nausea/vomiting) should raise suspicion of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

diagnosis: History and findings strongly suggest acute angle-closure glaucoma of the right eye — an ocular emergency. The pain assessment (severe pain with nausea/vomiting, haloes, photophobia) is the key history clue prompting urgent escalation. The competency is a thorough pain history with red-flag recognition.

immediate: Take a structured pain history: severity (0-10), exact type and location, photophobia, associated nausea/vomiting and haloes
Recognise that severe eye pain with nausea/vomiting and haloes suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma
Treat this as an emergency: alert the doctor immediately and do not delay
Measure VA and IOP (expect markedly raised IOP on the affected side) and document
Do not instil any drops without the doctor's order
Stay with the patient, keep her calm, and document the pain assessment and findings
follow_up: Doctor to manage acute IOP reduction (e.g., medications, possible laser iridotomy)
Continue to monitor the patient closely while waiting for the doctor
Document triage time and escalation in the record
patient_education: Reassure her that help is being arranged urgently and to stay as calm as possible
Advise her not to rub the eye and to remain seated comfortably
Explain that the doctor will see her quickly because this is urgent
Avoid giving detailed prognosis — defer clinical explanation to the doctor

key_points: Uses a pain scale (0-10) and asks the exact type and location of pain
Asks about associated nausea/vomiting, haloes, and photophobia
Establishes the sudden onset and blurred vision
Recognises the red-flag symptom cluster during history taking
Measures and documents VA and IOP for both eyes
Notes the markedly raised IOP and reduced VA on the affected side
Does not delay escalation to perform extra tests

Identifies this as an ocular emergency
Understands the urgency and the need to alert the doctor immediately
Does not attribute the symptoms to a minor cause
